utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry that we've been pushed back into this tiny little shoe box, but the number one court was required for the initial appearance of an accused who surrendered the other day, and they needed a public gallery, and we were the only one which would fit in here. We are back in the other courtroom next week. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Berberkic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, before the break you told us about the disappearance of Halim Dedovic in a group in December 1992, and you mentioned that Fahrudin Malkic, nicknamed Baron, was in this group, and that Gojko Jokanovic mentioned that this detainee had called him afterwards. What exactly did Mr. Jokanovic tell you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he said exactly was that Baron called him on the telephone from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know this Baron yourself?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know Baron, but I was in the same room with him for a while - I cannot remember exactly when - and he was also in Room 16 where I was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on did you ever meet him again after your release, or did you meet any of his relatives?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met with him again. I heard that he never showed up anywhere again and that he's registered as a missing person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember who told me that, but I discussed with him several people. Some of them even called me on the phone, some members of his family, but I cannot remember who it was exactly that I talked to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Dedovic, was he ever seen alive or met by you or anyone else; do you know? We talked about him.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Halim Dedovic is registered as missing. He has not been heard of ever. In Sarajevo, I talked to some people who inquired about him, they were his friends from Foca, but they couldn't tell me any news about him. He is missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this group you have mentioned that there was Aziz Sahinovic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he worked in a bank in Foca. I called him Banka, although I don't know whether that is accurate. He was with me in Room 18 when he was taken away. He was beaten several times. I think it was about some money. I think they wanted him to reveal the whereabouts of some Deutschemarks from the bank. And he was taken away with Medin Tatarevac who also worked in this bank. He disappeared with the same group. He personally told me that he, Jovo Savic, a guard, beat him up on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Mr. Sahinovic beaten by this guard Savic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the beginning, when he was just brought in. It could have been June, early June maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see injuries on Mr. Sahinovic after these beatings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw swellings, haematoma around both eyes. That is all you could see on his face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he was beaten on several occasions. How often was he beaten?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was more than two or more than three times. Perhaps three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it always the guard Savic who beat him or was that only on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that it was always Jovo Savic, but it is certain that Jovo Savic beat him at least once and beat him hard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sahinovic tell you where he was beaten, or do you know from other sources or your own observation where he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had been beaten in the solitary cell where he had spent some time, but he didn't say which solitary cell, whether it was the one within the compound, which means in building number 3, or it was one of the solitary cells in the administration building. That remained unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the case of Aziz Sahinovic is mentioned in the indictment under point 5.29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, do you know a Seval Soro?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think he was the one who was a butcher in Foca, but I couldn't give any precise information about him. I think he was there, but when he disappeared from the camp I could not confirm with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under C-24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Kemal Isanovic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Kemal Isanovic very well. He worked as a waiter in a pizzeria owned by Adnan Isanovic. I saw him on several occasions in the KP Dom. He was in building number 1. I don't know exactly in which room. He was interrogated several times, and I observed on him standard injuries to the face caused by a beating with a blunt object, such as swelling on the face, swelling around the eyes. I didn't notice any other injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under Schedule B, number 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Resad Hadzimesic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resad Hadzimesic, also known as Mesa, I know the man well. I played football with him in the local football club Sutjeska. He was in the KP Dom. I don't think that he had been beaten. I didn't notice any injuries on him at least. He was taken away from the KP Dom. I don't know exactly when, but I never heard of him since.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under B-24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, was a Mehmed Sofradzija detained in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mehmed Sofradzija is a distant relative of mine. He worked in the town hall before the war in Foca. He had been brought in from Novi Sad, as far as I know, and I believe that is accurate information. He was brought by policemen from Foca, one of them Matovic, who was the goalkeeper of the football club Sutjeska. I know him also. And he spent some time in solitary cells near the gate. I don't know how much time, but I believe it was five or six days. Later he was brought to building number 3. I don't know which room. I think it might have been Room 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he beaten? Could you see anything on him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was beaten and beaten badly. I believe his entire face was swollen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see him and where did you see him with these injuries?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him several times in the KP Dom. I think it was the month of July. He was there in July. I even saw him the last time he was taken away from the KP Dom. I communicated with him through the window, letting him know that he should telephone my family and tell them that I was alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean you thought he was going for an exchange and would be able to contact your family when you saw him last?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because at that moment, we thought that the prisoners who were leaving the camp were going for an exchange - at least that is the explanation we got from the guards who came to fetch the prisoners - or that they were going to do some work outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Mehmed Sofradzija taken away? When did you see him last?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been the first half of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he taken -- was he taken in a group of people, or was he taken alone?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken away in a group. I don't know how many people there were in the group, but it might have been more than ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear anything about this group later on?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, none of them were heard of since. I talked to his brother who lives in Sarajevo. He is still searching for him, although there is no new information available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mehmed Sofradzija, does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His nickname was Mesa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have opportunity to talk to him and ask him who beat him and where he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have occasion to talk to him directly. All the communication I had with him was through the window while he was leaving when I made the request that I had just mentioned. But I talked to another prisoner who was with him in a solitary cell, and that man's name is Asim. I don't remember the last name, but he comes from the village of Sukovac on the left bank of the Drina River. The solitary cells were in building number 3. The two of them were alone in the cell. Asim said that Mesa was very frightened because he didn't think he would survive. He took off the watch from his hand to -- and gave it to Asim so that Asim could give it to his son as a memento. He told Asim that he had been in a solitary cell for about seven days, one of the cells near the gates, and in that time he had nothing to eat or drink. He drank his own urine, those were his own words. Asim told me this story in Room 16 when he was brought to that room from a solitary cell. He didn't say who had beaten him. He only said in Novi Sad he was handcuffed, and his wrists and hands were swollen, and that this policeman Matovic was involved in all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the person Mehmed Sofradzija is mentioned under B-52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet a Salko Mandzo in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a man whose nickname was Kelta; Salko Mandzo, also known as Kelta. I never met him personally. He worked in a labour group, as far as I know. But in the beginning, in June, he was taken away several times and beaten near the gates in one of those cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? How do you know that? You said you did not meet him personally. Did you see him being taken and with injuries?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him both when he was being taken away and when he was being returned. I saw injuries on his face. At the time he was in building number 1. He was taken away several times and brought back. The prisoners who were with me told me that that was his name. I hadn't known him. And it later turned out that he was beaten by mistake, that he had been confused with somebody else. That is, at least, what I was told. Somebody else was supposed to be taken for a beating, not him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that it was in June, June 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was June in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you saw injuries on his face. Could you see what kind of injuries he had?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those injuries were probably inflicted by a hand or a blunt object. There was no bleeding that I can remember, at least, no significant bleeding. Those were mainly swellings and haematomas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he was beaten by mistake. Mistake for whom, do you know? Did you later learn for whom he was mistaken?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never learnt anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This pattern of beatings, how did they affect you personally? Psychologically, I mean.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It affected not only me but all the other prisoners. We were frightened for our lives. People who were beaten and who would come back to their rooms were in a very bad mental and physical state. Everyone in the room was frightened. We were thinking that we might be next, and we were even preparing for it. We had our own ways of preparing for it, namely, that people -- we used to give people who were being taken for interrogation our jackets to soften the blows that they were receiving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way did you prepare for, for your interrogation or for your turn? Did you do anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also received a sweater from another prisoner which I put on. I expected that I would be beaten. I wrote a farewell letter to my family and gave it to Hasan Dzano who was in my room, and I told him if he survived, he should find a way to deliver this letter to my wife and children. I was not optimistic about my chances of survival, at least, not in the beginning of my imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned two of your relatives that were in the KP Dom. Were more of your relatives in the KP Dom? Do you recall anyone else who was also detained with you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two of my relatives in there. One of them was Adnan Berberkic. He is from Miljevina. The other is Rasim Merkez from the village of Ribari near Josanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to these two of your relatives? Did they survive the KP Dom? Are they alive?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them survived. They're both missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us in the beginning of your testimony that you were arrested with Halil Merkez. What became of him? Did he survive the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He survived the KP Dom. He was exchanged. I think he was taken first to Kalinovik, where he spent some time in prison, and then he was exchanged. He now lives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned Adnan Dzaferspahic was arrested soon after you. What became of him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adnan Dzaferspahic did not survive the camp. He is registered as missing. He was taken away in a group of more than 30 men, all of whom were young men from 25 to 35 years old, strong men, able-bodied. The guards said they were taking them to do some sort of work. That was the explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this happen? When did he disappear from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could have been the first half of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described to us already how you were beaten in the yard by soldiers. Did you see any other detainee being beaten in the yard or in the canteen? Do you recall anyone?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a man who was ill; I think he had epilepsy. In front of the kitchen on the stairs, I think he was asking to go home. He was screaming, "I want to go home. Why am I here? I want to go home." Two guards, Vlatko Pljevaljcic and another one named Perisic, beat him and kicked him there on the stairs and then they brought him to building number 3. They beat him again in the hallway of that building. I don't know whether they returned him after that to his own room or to a solitary cell. I think he was brought back to his room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw that happen? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Room 16, and we could clearly see through the window of our room what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this person, the victim?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his name was Dzafer Humic, but I'm not sure, Humic, because I did not know him before nor did I have occasion to meet with him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he suffered from epilepsy. Did he also have a physical handicap?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember if he had trouble walking or if he had any other disability, but I think he was -- he had a disease of the nerves. I would call him a mental patient or a nervous patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that it is the incident 5.9 in the indictment and that the guards mentioned, Pljevaljcic is listed as number 35 in Exhibit P-3, and Perisic is listed under number 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever registered by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated that my name does not feature on any official lists nor did I have any occasion to see my name on the lists of organisations such as the Red Cross or any other humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ICRC come to the KP Dom and, if so, where were you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay at the KP Dom, the International Red Cross came twice. The first time, it was on the 23rd of June, 1992. No, 1993. I'm sorry. The second time, it was August the same year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you when they came?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, on the 23rd of June, 1992 [sic], a group of us were put into a vehicle, 12 of us. We were put into a car, and they took us to the basement of the bakery that was near the KP Dom. They took us in the morning. We stayed there until the afternoon, approximately. There were 12 of us. Witness FWS-111 was there; Dr. Torlak, Aziz Torlak; Witness FWS-146. I know that we were 12 in all. There were other detainees there too as well. We spent a certain amount of time there, so the guard who was guarding us took us back to the KP Dom on foot. He was armed. We queued up two by two, and he took us to the KP Dom, to the main gate. However, very soon, one of the policemen ran out of the outpost there and verbally attacked this guard, saying why did he bring us back when he had not received orders to that effect. So then we were quickly returned to the basement of the bakery. In front of the gate of the KP Dom, we saw a Land Rover with Red Cross signs on it. Obviously we had been hidden, and the guard who was guarding us there in hiding did not know why we had been hidden. Only in the evening we were picked up again and taken back to the room where we had been earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that the witness again said 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to clarify that. You said 23rd of June, 1992. Is that correct, or is it a mistake in the year?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's the 23rd of June, 1993. I think I said it. I think I also corrected myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said in August 1993 the Red Cross came again. Where were you? What happened?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August 1993 we found out from some guards that the International Red Cross would come. The detainees were even cleaning the premises in order to prepare for this visit by the Red Cross. However, in the morning we were picked up again on that same day. We were put into a military truck. They put us up on the truck. They closed the truck. Vlatko Pljevaljcic, an armed guard, was on the truck with us. They drove us to Brioni. That is a locality on the right bank of the Cehotina. It's about three or four kilometres away from Foca. There was a farm there before the war and also during the war, and they had some kind of agricultural produce there. We were put into a hangar, something like that, and they told us to clean up the chicken coops where there were chickens before the war. We stayed there the whole day. There were 12 of us again. Actually, it was the same group of people that had been hidden in the basement of the bakery. Around dusk, we were returned again, and at the parking space in front of Brioni we saw the same Land Rover belonging to the Red Cross, and we had assumed that they had already returned from their visit to the KP Dom, and that proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I would be interested to know something about the makeup of this group of 12, the same group of 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you would like to ask some questions about that, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned several of the people that are on your list and you have already mentioned Dr. Torlak. The other people in this group, what kind of people were they?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that these were intellectuals, although Witness FWS-146 was among them who did not really belong to this group of intellectuals, I should say. Professor Husein Lojo was there; Safet Avdic, a director; I already mentioned Witness FWS-111; and I think there was Witness FWS-71.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that except for the one person 146, they were all intellectuals. Were you prominent citizens, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were intellectuals and prominent citizens of Foca, well-known people, business people who enjoyed a high reputation and people who also held various high offices in Foca. We were wondering why we were isolated at all, the 12 of us, why we were isolated into that room, and we assumed that this might have meant some kind of preparations for an exchange. Actually, we were afraid that we were a group that was being manipulated in different ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were isolated. Does that mean the 12 of you were kept separate, in a separate room in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right. We were kept in a separate room in building number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since when were you in this isolated position?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After director Dzevad Lojo left - he was the director of the mine in Miljevina - that was in March 1993, after that they established this group of the 12 of us, and they put us in a separate room in building number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with any of the KP Dom staff about why you were separated?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke to many guards who guarded us, but nobody could give us reliable information. They were simply guessing, just like we were. That's what they told us, we are preparing you for -- "They are preparing you for something," but we did not know what it was all about, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Dr. Berberkic, let us now talk about some people -- some staff members of the KP Dom. Who was the warden of the KP Dom while you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, the warden was Milorad Krnojelac, Mico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the prewar warden?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warden was another Serb who I knew very well, but right now I can't remember his name. I may be able to remember it later, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- this other person who was the warden before Mr. Krnojelac, did you see him in the KP Dom while you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw that person, although I know that person well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with anyone of the KP Dom staff about this former warden and why he was replaced?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Radojica Tesovic. He was the warden of the KP Dom before the war broke out. We talked to the guards. We even talked amongst ourselves as to what had happened to him, why he had left. We received information from the Serb guards that allegedly he did not agree with SDS policy and that he refused the position of warden of the KP Dom that had been offered to him and that he went to be the director of the farm at Brioni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you? You said "guards," but who?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I put this? A person I was on good terms with, and that person is a [redacted], but I cannot give you [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he could get into trouble because of his role in all of this or his behaviour towards the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be willing to write his name on a piece of paper so that we would not mention this person but see the name on the paper?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That name would have to be shown to the accused. You understand that, do you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is a real problem. I mean I'm not saying against the accused himself, but if there is a perception that he could get into trouble, then it may be that we will have to just avoid the use of his name, unless it is in some way important to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I thought it is important, but we have to ask the witness if under this condition he is willing to write down the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think he has said no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He said it was a problem. He said, "No. I was not aware of that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps I was observing his body language, but you better ask him directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under what you have now been told, are you still willing to write his name down or do you not want to do it now, knowing that the accused would get this information?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave - I believe that my learned friend will agree with me - in his statement that we have and that the accused has, this witness already gave this name. So he said who he got this information from. I'll give you the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's very good of you, Mr. Bakrac, to point that out. I think, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, in those circumstances there could be no problem, provided that it is not made public. But the statements cannot be made public. And indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was going to say, Mr. Bakrac, that they have been given to you on the basis that you don't make them public beyond what is necessary for the purpose of investigating the case. So if it's in the statement, it is still not public but it is, nevertheless, in the hands of the accused. Do you want to add something to what you said before?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I just wanted to help where this is. I mean in the B/C/S version, it's page 9. As for the English version, it's page 10. That's where mention is made of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What I see actually in the statement is he mentioned a person who gave him information about the KP Dom and incidents in the KP Dom, but he did not mention that this person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He was a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. He did not mention that this person told him about why Mr. Tesovic was replaced. Therefore, I wasn't really aware of--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see. It might be a good idea if you showed the witness his statement so that we can get this cleared up before anything further is said by him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness his statement. It's ID number, in the binder, 326, and in the B/C/S version, it's page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Page 9, he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Please, if you show Dr. Berberkic this page of his statement. It's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look -- when you look right in the middle of this page, you find a sentence referring to information you got from a person in the KP Dom. Do you see this name?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In those circumstances, I think that if we could have that person's name written on a piece of paper - I don't want to put the statement in evidence - and it can go in under seal so that we have the record straight, but it certainly will not be made public.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, did you hear what the Presiding Judge said?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think for safety's sake we should redact the answer, lines 23 and 24. The document will be Exhibit P438, and it will be under seal. The passage I am having redacted, you've seen that, have you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but I really didn't understand why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because if that was made public, it would demonstrate precisely what it is we say the doctor does not want to have --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Now I understand. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's just to protect the person's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do beg your pardon for interrupting, but I think that after all of this, it would be right if the Defence would see what is written on this piece of paper. We assume that it is what we have all been talking about, but we would like to have a look, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm sorry. I didn't realise it had been kept from you. Of course you may see it [redacted] [redacted] Thank you. Having said that, that sentence will have to be redacted as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, you said that the warden, during your confinement, was Mr. Krnojelac. Do you know -- did you get information who appointed Mr. Krnojelac in this position?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed that amongst the prisoners in the camp, and we had some information that allegedly it was the military command, the military command that had appointed Krnojelac warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of information was that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room that I was in, Room 16, there were people who knew Krnojelac and who expressed interest, who perhaps wanted to talk to him to discuss our position, to look into why we had been detained, and to find ways and means of improving our situation. I think that these people had better information than the rest, including myself. I'm referring to Dzevad Lojo, the director of the mine at Miljevina. The other Dzevad Lojo, the director of Maglic, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the prison staff members confirm this, or was it just the talk and the information that the detainees had?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, nor can I say for sure, whether any of the guards had confirmed this piece of information. I think that I personally Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in conversation with Gojko Jokanovic, that actually I talked to him about this for two or -- on two or three occasions. He confirmed that the military command had appointed Krnojelac. But as for the guards, I did not talk ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you had this conversation with Gojko Jokanovic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Krnojelac from before the war?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I did not know him, nor did I ever see him before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him several times. Many times, I should say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that this was Mr. Krnojelac when you didn't know him from before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guards told me -- or people told me, rather, detainees who were in Room 16, they told me. They knew him well. Some of them had worked with him, others had social contacts, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him in the prison, what did he wear?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in an olive-green/gray uniform. He wore a cap. I think it was the type of cap called Titovka or Partizanka, whichever. I think he had a pistol in a holster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this cap. Did a special group of soldiers wear this cap, or was it just the usual cap that all soldiers wore?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the type of cap that was worn by the partisans in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him in the military uniform, did you see any insignia, rank insignia on the uniform or the cap?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say with any degree of certainty. I believe it had some signs of rank, but I cannot really confirm this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that he was the warden? What information did you have that he was the warden at that time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that we had requested improvements in our conditions and that we were looking for a contact with someone who was in charge of us, who would explain why we were there, what our status was. And we always got one and the same answer, that he was the one responsible; he could help get an improvement in our position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what times did you see him in the KP Dom? You said you saw him often. At what times?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at various times. In the beginning, the mess where we had our meals was also used by the staff, by guards and other staff, so in the beginning, in July and June also, he also came along with guards and had his breakfast and lunch in that mess. So it was mainly in the morning hours during the day and sometimes even in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned June and July. Is that, again, 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after, after this -- after June, July 1992, did you continue to see him going for meals into the canteen, or did that stop?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that didn't happen often. At least, it happened more rarely afterwards. But they had so-called alarms in the camp, and I think three such alarms happened in the camp during my stay there. And on those occasions, all guards and the administration staff would arrive fully armed and fully equipped to the compound, to the KP Dom, and then we could see them within the compound wearing camouflage or normal military uniforms, it depends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did these alarms take place? Do you recall the month when that happened?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. The first one was in December 1992. The second one, the second alert or alarm was when Zekovic escaped, and that was in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third one?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember about the third one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think that could have been the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the staff then came fully armed. What did that mean? What do you mean by fully armed? What did you see on the staff members?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore military uniforms or camouflage uniforms that they had made themselves, and they had automatic rifles and a full warfare of equipment, wearing caps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they do when you saw them? The alarm, what did that include?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would usually place soldiers, in fact, the guards who toured the camp, they would place them in front of the buildings where we were locked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac taking part in such alarms?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw him do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was present, especially during the second alert when Zekovic had run away, and I think that he gave assignments to and issued orders to the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he present during the first alarm, that is, autumn 1992? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in December 1992, on this second alarm?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: December 1992 was the first alert or alarm that I remember, and the second one was when Zekovic ran away. I think you made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then the first alarm that you remember, December 1992, was Mr. Krnojelac present, and, if so, what did you see him do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember about the first alert, whether he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the second alert in relation to Mr. Zekovic, was Mr. Krnojelac also fully armed, as you said?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was present there, and I believe that everyone had automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on this occasion, this second occasion related to Zekovic? What did you see happen? Where were you and what did you see happen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Zekovic escaped on an afternoon, and it could have been the beginning of July 1993. Whether it was the 4th or the 7th, I can't remember, but I believe it was the 7th of July, 1993. When they found out that he had escaped, they turned on a siren. So we found out that something had happened, and very soon we could see guards running out into the compound, carrying automatic weapons. They were probably looking for clues to find out where he could have gone. They were searching the inner area of the camp. They withdrew the working group from the working area and put them back into their rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that day, but the next day, when Ekrem Zekovic was captured, that's when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Where were you when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were lined up on the stadium within the compound. All of us prisoners from all rooms were lined up. First of all, we were taken out into the yard. Ekrem Zekovic was standing in front of us at a distance of about five or six metres. Savo Todovic, also known as Bunda, was standing behind him, together with Milorad Krnojelac, nicknamed Mico, and all the guards of the KP Dom were also present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what happened in the yard?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Todovic made a speech. He said approximately the following, and I think I got this right. I remember it well. He said, "You have in front of you Ekrem Zekovic who tried to escape from the concentration camp or the prison, as you call it, but he didn't succeed. He was captured in a village by women and children. No form of violence has been applied to him, which is another proof of the humaneness of the Serbian army. We know that this attempt is just a test balloon for organised escape which is being prepared by intellectuals, but you don't stand a chance of escaping. "From this day on, your rations will be cut down by half. All medical care is banned, and that means that even Dr. Berberkic shall not be allowed to help any of the prisoners. Any conversation with guards is, hence, forbidden. Looking through the window is forbidden. "And now you will all go back to your rooms, collect all the medication and any other things that do not belong to you, and the guards will come to collect them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Todovic gave this speech, where was Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was standing right next to him with the group of guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he respond or react in any way to what Mr. Todovic said?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did not utter a word, but he showed his approval by nodding his head. But he didn't actually say a word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were returned to your rooms, did all of what Mr. Todovic mention -- let's call it collective punishment, did all this actually happen? Were the rations halved, was the medicine taken away, were you not allowed any longer to help other detainees?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as we entered the rooms, the guards arrived perhaps 20 minutes later and collected all the things that we had. We turned over some medicines, some cigarettes, all the things that we used and all the things that we made ourselves to make our lives a little easier, all the written material that we had prepared, all the books. Anything that we had, they took away. On that day, we did not receive any food. As far as I can remember, we did not receive food on the day when Zekovic escaped, the entire next day, and then the day after, we got only breakfast and we got only half rations compared to the rations we got before, and I think these half rations continued for about a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you saw Mr. Krnojelac on other occasions in the KP Dom. Did you ever see him in the evening?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did come to the administration building of the camp and to the compound in the evenings. I don't remember if I personally saw him within the compound, but I believe he did come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the basis of your belief?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the behaviour of the guards who were guarding us. They told us they had to be careful with us because the warden is in the building, as they put it, or within the compound; on the grounds, in fact. That meant that we had to be quiet, that we had to watch our step, that we shouldn't communicate with the guards, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that said? Do you recall when the guards made such remarks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened throughout my stay there. It depended on the guards. Some of them were less brave, some of them were braver, but all of them had this fear of the warden. While I was there, it was true for the entire duration of my stay, so there is no particular period when that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the guards had this fear of the warden. Can you be more specific? Did they fear him, or respect him, or how did it -- can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were afraid they might make an error, a misstep, and that they would be punished for that misstep by being sent to the front line. There were guards among them who were less brutal, as I would say, and they were unpopular with the warden, and they were afraid of being sent to the front line because of that, so they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that those guards who treated you less brutal were unpopular with the warden? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them who was helping us, who helped many of us, was sent to the front line maybe 15 days later, and we noticed immediately that he was no longer around, and we made inquiries about him. But he returned very soon. Sometime, I believe it was the Christmas of 1993, I was in Room 18. The guards had gathered in the guards' room in building number 3. They drank all night, sang, and talked among themselves, and I heard that guards Maric and Ivanovic were there. I recognised their voices. You couldn't see anything because it was dark, but I heard their voices. They discussed among themselves the situation in the camp, their positions and the position of the prisoners. It was obvious they'd had quite a lot to drink. And then they quarreled. I heard Guard Maric say the following, I heard him clearly: "What do I care? I didn't beat anyone or kill anyone; you did." And he also said, "Somebody will answer for this."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This Guard Maric, Your Honour, is the person listed under 103 on the list P-3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure whether the witness has answered your question yet, but it may be best if we come back to it after the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We still want to know why this is tied in with the accused. Your question was, "How do you know that those guards who treated you less brutally were unpopular with the warden? How do you know that?" Now, we've been told that somebody was sent off to the front line and came back after a short time, but there would need to be, if you want to rely upon this, something more than what the witness has already said. Anyway, we'll come back to it at 11.30. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid that our delay was caused by the fact that the next witness requires some protective measures and it's rather difficult to organise them for this courtroom, but I think we've got it sorted out. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you had mentioned that some guards were unpopular with the warden and they were afraid to be sent to the front line. My question was: How do you know that they were unpopular with the warden? You have given us an example of one who was actually sent to the front line, but can you add to this question to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think they were strictly prohibited from talking to us and helping us. I was guarded in prison by five of my neighbours who were guards as well. I tried to get in touch with them, but sometimes I did manage to, sometimes I did not. One of them would occasionally give a piece of bread to me on the sly, but he told me that I had to keep quiet about this, that I shouldn't tell anyone about it, that I should be very cautious. Sometimes we only signalled to each other with our eyes, hands, various movements. Sometimes we would actually communicate in words; we would actually have a conversation. However, any communication that existed between me and the guards is something that we tried to keep secret somehow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how do you know that these guards who were less brutal and who had these forbidden communications, how do you know that they were unpopular with the warden, that is, Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My two neighbours told me directly that they were -- that it was forbidden to them to communicate with us and that they could get into trouble if they would give me a slice of bread or something like that. Gojko Jokanovic also repeated that several times. When we tried to stop him somewhere in the compound or to ask him for some kind of help, he would just wave his hand and say, "I can't. I can't. Go away. Please don't get me into trouble," things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how do you know that Mr. Krnojelac was actually the one who would be involved in consequences for them? Did they say something like this or is it your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said directly that they could have trouble with the administration. That's what they said. Not the warden himself but the administration. That pertains to these guards and Gojko himself, that they could get into trouble with the administration. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that one of the guards was actually sent to the front line. Which guard and when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the guard who helped me before and who I mentioned earlier on. I don't know exactly when this happened, but we had received information that they were taking shifts at the front line every 15 days. I don't know whether that's true, actually, but I think it's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have also described a situation when you heard the Serb guards discuss and drink on Christmas, on Christmas 1993. Do you mean the Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the 6th of January, 1993. I remember that it was Christmas because the next morning we went for breakfast and one of the guards gave me some brandy to drink, a gulp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the guard Maric that you actually heard specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made a mistake. It's not the guard number 103, it's 102 on the list. 103 is a lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know to whom he made this remark, that "you killed"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the guard Obrenovic was with them then, and also some other guards, but I'm sure about these two and Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Obrenovic is listed under number 46 on P-3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You actually gave this -- told us about this Christmas conversation that you overheard in response, actually, to my question about the less brutal guards and their being unpopular. How does that relate to this issue?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to this case that occurred, or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, my question was -- at that point in time my question was how do you know that guards were unpopular with the warden and that they had to go to the front line. And then you told us this incident from Christmas Eve, and I was wondering, how does that relate? Because you gave that as a response to my question. Or is it just that it came to your mind at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that you ask him whether that guard who gave him the gulp of brandy said something to him of what would happen if that had been found out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard what the Presiding Judge said. Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that because I don't understand any of this. I just can't. I think that these are broader concepts that are involved. It's not easy to answer this question. In my opinion, the most difficult period in the KP Dom was June, July, August, September 1992. This case, this incident that occurred later -- I mean, I think that the situation had changed completely by then. Why? I can't say. I can't say why the situation changed in prison, but I think that there was a differentiation amongst the guards themselves for I don't know what reasons, and I know that they often quarreled among themselves. Those guards who were nicer to us quarreled with those who were more brutal to us. Why that happened, I truly don't know. The situation was probably developing in an unfavourable direction for them. Of course, I know that this Court works according to certain rules and on the basis of proof that is presented. However, the attitude of guards towards prisoners varied. Sometimes it was extremely brutal on the part of individual guards, and sometimes they were softer. That depended on many things, on the situation in the camp and on the situation in general. So I think that you have to view the camp as a whole throughout its existence, not a certain period that is more brutal and another period that is less brutal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, let me stop you here and let's move on. You said that -- no. Did you see Mr. Krnojelac also in the camp on weekends, or was he there during the working days only?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether he came during the weekend. I cannot say for sure whether he was present during weekends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, who -- was he alone, or was usually someone with him, and if so, who?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was mainly in the company of two persons. One is Savo Todovic, nicknamed Bunda, and the other one is Mitar Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Todovic's exact function in the KP Dom, do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that he was in charge of the detainees and everything that had to do with the detainees. I'm referring to the status in prison, their work, discipline. He was the one who decided who would be in the work group, who would go out, who would work inside, who would work in which part of the building. I think that he was basically the operations man, the person in charge of the operation of the prison. He is the one who decided who would go into solitary confinement, how long he would stay in solitary confinement, and probably who would be beaten, and other things that had to do with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Todovic, in this function as the operation man, did he have dealings with all detainees, that is, the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think so. He was in charge of the Serb prisoners just like he was in charge of the Muslims, the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore an olive-green/grey uniform, and he wore a sheepskin jacket, the same colour, with a black collar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "olive-green/grey uniform," do you mean military uniform?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you saw Krnojelac together with him. Could you see -- from what you saw, could you make out who was superior, Todovic or Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? What do you mean when you say "superior"? In relation to one another was one the superior of the other, or are you referring to something different?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I was referring to, if you could see anything in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Krnojelac was Savo Todovic's superior or, actually, quite directly, I think Todovic carried out Krnojelac's orders or instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you form this opinion? Did you see anything or is it just their position, their official positions? Did you see, for instance, Krnojelac ordering Todovic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No, not directly, but I think that the organisation of the camp, of the prison, was such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already described to us that you had this one occasion with Mr. Todovic after you had taken bread. Did you have -- were there other occasions that you spoke with Mr. Todovic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to him on another occasion too. That was in Room 16, the beginning. It could have been September or the autumn of 1992. I was exhausted at the time. I couldn't walk. I was totally exhausted. I vomited several times. I also had diarrhea. I could hardly walk. Through a guard, I asked to talk to him. He talked to me very briefly in building number 3, in the guards' room. He wore an olive-green/grey uniform, and he was also wearing that leather jacket then. I asked him to transfer me to that working group, but he said he couldn't. He primarily talked to me about my brother who was in Sarajevo at the time. He said that my brother is one of the guards or the deputy warden in the Ustasha camp -- Ustasha prison in Sarajevo - that's the way he had put it - and that he was in very active in the Ustasha movement in Sarajevo. I told him, in response to that, that I knew my brother very well and that this is completely false, that these are mere fabrications. We talked on our own. The guard was waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you want to be transferred to the working group?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two reasons. One was to get a slice of bread. The second one was for me to try to find out what was going on outside, because people who were in the work group managed to get out, which was inconceivable for us then. We called that the information blockade, and that was very hard on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were detainees afraid of Mr. Todovic? Were you afraid of him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all the prisoners were afraid of him. Whenever he appeared in the compound, we were terrified, and we always watched to see which part of the prison, which building he would go to, and we would always be pleased if we would see that he was not going into our building, because we knew that he had great power and that he could decide on everything that had to do with the prisoners and that he had great influence within the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the guards?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Mitar Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the prison on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he wear?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that he changed uniforms. At first he had a military uniform, an olive-green/grey one. Later he changed that uniform for a uniform that was worn by the policemen before the war. Those are those blue uniforms with light-blue shirts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he start wearing this blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was -- it could have been 1993, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Rasevic attend to both the Serb and the Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that he had something to do with the Muslims; however, I'm not sure about the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever talk with Mr. Rasevic while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to him twice, the first time when I was in Room 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that about, approximately?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been the autumn of 1992. They came every night to take the count of the prisoners, as they had put it. We would line up. The guard on duty would come, and then Mitar Rasevic came with one of the guards. They counted us. He called out to me. He singled me out of the group; he wanted to talk to me. He talked to me very briefly. He mostly talked about the situation in the KP Dom before the war because he was a good friend of my brother's. He said how the Serbs and the Muslims at the KP Dom parted their ways peacefully, and that that was probably thanks to my brother and Radojica Tesovic. I asked him about the possibility of exchanges. He couldn't say anything, neither yes nor no. He did not talk about these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain, can you --

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the second time too, I think. The second time I talked to him was just before I was taken off for an exchange on the 12th of August, 1993. He came into the room. At that time I was in building number 3. He walked in after breakfast, and he said that I should get my things. He said that I was going for an exchange to Sarajevo, and that I should give his regards to my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is all we said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, let me stop you. I would like to need -- I would need an explanation. You said about the first meeting you had with him, you said, at least it's in the transcript, "He said how the Serbs and the Muslims of the KP Dom parted their ways peacefully, and that that was probably thanks to my brother and Radojica Tesovic." Can you explain that? I do not really understand this sentence. What do you mean -- or what did he mean?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he held my brother in high regard for several reasons. As for the event that he referred to, it actually did take place. I think that he was even at the KP Dom at that time. Sometime in the beginning of April 1992, that is to say, before the conflict broke out, at the KP Dom they had a meeting. The entire staff, the Serbs and the Muslims, talked trying to resolve how they would part, how they would overcome this problem. At any rate, they parted peacefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police that was there, Serb and -- Serbs and Muslims, they could all decide where they wanted to go. They parted peacefully. They all wore police uniforms, and they could all carry their respective weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We do not need to go into more details. I was just wondering to what Mr. Rasevic was referring. Yes, thank you, but you have clarified the matter. Did you ever complain to him on this occasion when you talked with him on the first occasion, did you complain about the living conditions or the beatings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I talked to him I mentioned it, but he said that was not within his jurisdiction. He said something like this: "That was the jurisdiction of the warden, and the warden was the only one who could decide to improve our position," meaning the possibility of improving the food, availability of medical care, et cetera. But he made it clear that it was not within his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards in the KP Dom, were they the regular prison guards from before the war, or were there also other people doing guard duty?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the majority were men who worked in the KP Dom before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the guards wear?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very complex question, really. It depended. In the beginning when the camp was established, when I arrived there in May, June, and even July, August, and September, I would say they wore military uniforms, grey olive, and they carried automatic weapons, in order to switch later to camouflage uniforms. And some of them, for instance -- Guard Micevic wore the real Chetnik uniform, including the cap with the cockade. One of the guards, I think it was Milenko Burilo, wore for a while the uniform of the old Yugoslav army. I remember we were wondering where he got hold of that uniform. I believe after the new year in 1993, in January, they switched back to the uniforms worn by the police before the war in the KP Dom. When I went to be exchanged in August 1993, I remember they wore the blue uniforms worn before the war by the staff, the guards of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the person mentioned is Micevic. He is not on the list of the staff members, P-3, and Burilo is number 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards, did they attend to all the detainees, that is, the Serbs and the Muslims, or were certain guards only dealing with the Serbs and others only with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in charge of all the prisoners, both groups. I know that because the same guard opened the doors of our rooms and led us out to have our meals, and he also led out the Serbian prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards, did they always work on the same post or did the same guards sometimes work in the prisoners' quarters or in the administration building? Did they switch? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they only changed the schedule, the duty roster, within the compound, and some guards did not work in the administrative building at all. They did not perform any administrative duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, for instance, say where Burilo worked? What was his special post, if you are able to say so?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not precisely define his workplace. I think he spent most of his time in the compound. I don't think, for instance, he was in charge of buildings 1, 2, or 3. He walked around the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the guard Obrenovic that you also mentioned, where did he work? What did you see -- in which posts did you see him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guard Obrenovic was mainly in charge of building number 2. While I was there in Room 16 and 18, he would often come to unlock the door and take us out. And when I was in Room 16, sometime at the end of June or July, he came to me in Room 16 to ask for crutches for Zijad Subasic. I had some crutches, and he took them from me, saying that he needed them. In any case, he spent most of his time in the guards' room in building number 2, although I believe it depended on their duty roster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described to us various beatings, especially the beatings in the second half of June 1992. Did you observe guards being involved in these beatings? Would you be able to name guards who were involved in this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the guards who took out prisoners in that period were the same guards who beat them, mainly in solitary cells in the administrative building. We could only hear cries for help and voices of both the guards and the victims. We could not see clearly through the windows which guards they were - we couldn't recognise them - but we could see through the window - and I did on several occasions - arms being raised to hit someone either with a hand or with a baton, but we couldn't tell which guards they were. I think it is difficult to claim with any degree of certainty as to who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the guards who took out these particular detainees?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the guards well. I believe Obrenovic took out a large number of detainees; that a guard whom we called Zuti, which means yellow, and his name was Dragan, took out a group of people, calling out names from a list, and he did not appear for a while in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he did not appear for a while in the prison, does that mean when the beatings started he did not appear or do you actually mean a real time period, weeks? What do you mean by "a while"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He read out the names and took out this group of people in mid-September 1992. He took them to the so-called plum picking, and after that, he didn't appear in the prison for two months. It was our conclusion that he had gone with that group. We couldn't understand why he wasn't in the prison any more. That's the period I'm talking about. In June 1992, prisoners were mainly taken out by guards who were on shift at the time. I said earlier that I remember that Dragan Obrenovic had taken out a large number of people. Another guard was Vlatko Pljevaljcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have already mentioned Obrenovic. It's the person 46 on the list. And Pljevaljcic is number 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that Rasevic told you, you would be exchanged, and you have already mentioned that you were taken out of the KP Dom on the 12th of August, 1993. At that time was Mr. Krnojelac, was he still the warden, do you know; that is, on the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that the warden was still in place at the time. He was present when Ekrem Zekovic had escaped and was captured. It was July 1993, which means a month before my departure from the KP Dom, and at that time Krnojelac was still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see him before you left the KP Dom? In this last couple of days that you were in the KP Dom, was he still there? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken out of the KP Dom alone, or in a group of people?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken out. I was taken away alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me to the Kula prison near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "they," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two men in military uniforms, armed. They put me in a police vehicle, Volkswagon Golf. When they put me in the back seat of the car, one of them introduced himself. He said, "My name is Zeljko Samardzic, and I'm a Chetnik from Bileca." The other one said his name was Trivun. He didn't say his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who handed you over to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was guard Micevic. I was waiting to be taken for this exchange in that room in the reception area. I waited for about an hour, and it was guard Micevic who turned me over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Kula?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the conditions in Kula, were they similar to what you had experienced in Foca, or were they different?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in Kula there was more food than in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- after this month, were you exchanged in a group or again as a single person?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
