utterances.text: I was exchanged on the 12th of September, 1993, at night-time in the area of the Jewish cemetery. I was exchanged for an elderly married couple and a Serb from Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already described how you suffered while you were detained in the KP Dom. You have described your mental suffering and your physical suffering. Did you suffer any permanent mental or physical harm or, at least, some longer lasting after your release? Did you experience anything?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is difficult to describe now. There are two things which are a consequence of all that I had gone through at the camp. My physical health is very good and very stable, fortunately. I believe that there is a form of PTSD, post-traumatic stress syndrome, or the Vietnam syndrome as doctors refer to it, and in that respect I'm no exception compared to other detainees. But I'm suffering from another thing which has developed in my conscience as a result of my experience and suffering, and that is an undefiable desire to live and for better things in life, and an awareness that about 400 people who had been in the camp are missing, that they're no longer alive, and that their bodies will be revealed, found one day. Those are, perhaps, the thoughts that help me to preserve my sanity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, you said that you suffered post-traumatic stress syndrome. What did you actually -- what did you suffer? What did you notice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What are his symptoms?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the symptoms that you personally noticed to have?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suffer from a mental block in my thought process, and you may have noticed this. It tends to appear suddenly. I cannot predict when it will appear; it simply occurs. It may be caused, triggered, by something. I still have this fear when I see a police uniform or when I see a pistol. That happened to me both in Sarajevo, it keeps happening in the country where I live now, and it happened to me in this country and in this building, as a matter of fact. As for the traumatic experiences from the camp and what I have survived, of course I have flashbacks. But I wouldn't say, however, that my PTS syndrome is as pronounced as in some people with whom I have met later and who suffer much worse, and the reason why it is not that pronounced is precisely what I said about wanting to live, wanting to experience better things in life, and to transform my wartime experiences and experiences from the camp into something better, something more useful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Berberkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These are the questions that the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Mr. Bakrac, do you mind if I try explaining to the witness about the pause and see how we go? Doctor, you've noticed that when you have been listening to the translation in the earphones there that counsel who is asking you the questions has stopped speaking some time before the translation finishes. That's because the translators or the interpreters work about half a sentence behind the speaker. Now, you are going to be cross-examined by somebody who speaks the same language as you, and you will be able to hear the question in your own language. You won't have to wait for the translation, but the translators still have to keep on translating for us. So when you have heard the question from Mr. Bakrac here, would you please pause to enable the translators to catch up, the same as they were able to do so when you were pausing, waiting to answer the questions. So let's give them a chance to keep up with us and with you before you answer the question. Yes, Mr. Bakrac. Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Berberkic. This Trial Chamber has already told you my name, but I wish to introduce myself, nevertheless. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, and I am one of the defenders of the accused, Mr. Milorad Krnojelac. I will ask you a number of questions, and the Trial Chamber already explained that we should pause between questions and answers. First of all, I wish to ask you: Do you remember that on the 14th and 15th of December, 1998, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps I'll make this easier for you, and we'll proceed more quickly if I explain that this is the date of the interview, and the date when you signed it is the 7th of September, 1999. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave several statements. If that is the date that you have, it's probably accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was just going to tell you that -- to ask you whether on the 16th of September, 1993, you gave another statement to the security services centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that too is accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those statements read out to you and did you sign them voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read those statements, and I signed them of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberkic. Is it true that in your first statement, in the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor's office, you said that you performed your job before the war in the hospital and only after the war you began to support the Muslim cause? Is it true that you said that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what I said very well. I was asked whether I was a member of the SDA. I said that I was not a member of any political party, the SDA included. As for the question whether I support the SDA, I said that I was a supporter, and I think that you can interpret that any way you want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, the point of my questions is not for me to interpret things but for you to ascertain what you mean by "the Muslim cause." I looked at the English translation, which says that you became involved as a person supporting the Muslim cause. I'm asking you what this means. I don't want to infer anything. That is why I'm putting these questions to you.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used the term "the Muslim cause," never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, would it be helpful if I gave this to you? If my understanding is correct, you speak English. Perhaps I could give you the B/C/S version and the English version so that you can see it. You said that you read it and signed it voluntarily. Is it necessary for me to show this to you, actually?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can show it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: While that's being done, Mr. Bakrac, I don't want to sound like a broken record about this, but you know how these statements are taken. They're taken in B/C/S and translated into English, recorded into English. The witness signs the English version and then it is, for some reason, translated back into B/C/S by somebody else and that's the document you're given. So precise wording such as "the Muslim cause," goes through two sets of interpretations. It's not really of great importance to us. I accept what you say. Those words appear in the English version. That doesn't mean he used those words or even the precise words in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour, but then we really have a big problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've had that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has a big problem, you see, because everything we believe is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So do we. I mean it's something which, when I first found out this is the way the OTP took its statements, I said they should do something about changing it. Whether they ever have, I don't know. We haven't got up to any trials raised in statements that were taken after I first came here. But it is an absurd way in which the OTP takes the statements. We've pointed it out. We've pointed out the difficulties. But we're faced with the fact that that's the way they were taken in this case. I realise that even you have and we have the same one, but I don't think that you are assisting us or your client by dwelling upon precise words in the document which were signed. That's all I'm trying to point out to you. You show it to him if you wish to, but I don't want to waste too much time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. But sometimes a mistranslation or a misspoken sentence can have an entirely different meaning, so that's the reason. However, with your permission, in order to save time - and I don't think that the witness is bringing into question the fact that I'm telling the truth - could the witness just explain as briefly as possible what he meant by all of this, and I hope that we will save time that way. I believe that nobody is bringing this into question, including the Prosecutor, I mean, that what I read is true. Let the witness just explain what he meant when he said that, and we will deal with that very briefly, and then move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And if I may also remind you, it doesn't seem to help us very much. He voted for the -- as I recall, he voted for the separate state. What does that tell us? Does it mean we disbelieve his evidence? You know, you proceed. I think we're probably wasting more time discussing it. You ask him what he meant -- well, you asked him what his political views were. That's what you're really after, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Then I'm going to move on to my next question which may actually be related to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the hospital, did you join the Muslim forces in any way?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left the hospital, I went to Ustikolina twice. That's a place that's about 11 kilometres downstream on the left bank of the Drina. I went to the clinic where my colleagues worked. I got a sack full of medicines from the doctor who worked there, and I gave all of this to my neighbours in case they might need it. I'm not trying to hide this. I said this during my questioning. I voted for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was not a member of the SDA or of any political party, nor do I ever intend to be one in my life, although I come from a political family. My only intention and desire in life, and that's the way I behaved in the hospital as well and in the beginning of the war, is to help people, regardless of who they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you allow me, and I believe that the Court will allow me to do this as well, could you please answer my question specifically. I have to ask you that. My question is, did you try to organise a clinic in Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that in your statement on page 3 you said, "I helped the TO, the Territorial Defence, in Ustikolina to organise a clinic. From there I took a bag full of medicines and bandages to the units that were guarding the hills near the Drina in an area called Krcino Brdo."

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just took the medicines to these people, but I did not organise the clinic in Ustikolina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I read out to you is not correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only once at the clinic in Ustikolina. I did not organise the clinic in Ustikolina. I have to repeat this to you once again. I don't know how that got into that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that from this clinic in Ustikolina, you took a bag full of medicines and bandages to an area on the right bank of the Drina, an area called Krcino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, that is absolutely correct. I repeated that to you before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in combat when you took these medicines to the units there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you were issued a pistol with two belts of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to possibly protect myself or kill myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean, to protect yourself?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a pistol is not a weapon with which you can kill others in war, in conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, what's the calibre of that pistol?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a Duga Devetka, a long-barrelled 9. I don't really know what that means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know how to use a gun, a pistol?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the first time in my life that I had a pistol in my hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how to use this pistol?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew how to put the clip inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the binoculars, did you have those binoculars before the war, or were you issued these binoculars together with the pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the answer, who the binoculars belonged to before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may not have heard that. The interpreters are not clear as to just who it was the witness said the binoculars belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that the witness answered that the binoculars belonged to his father before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you would just ask him that directly so as we've got an answer on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, who did the binoculars that you used belong to, as you said during the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The binoculars belonged to my father. The binoculars were obtained before the war, some ten years before the war, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war conflict broke out, did the Muslims have some kind of organisation, and were they getting ready for what was to take place?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they did have some kind of organisation, but I did not participate in any political type of organising, and I think that they were very bad at organisation, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say "regrettably"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because everybody has the right to defend his or her state from a possible attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that this was not the state of the Serbs from that area?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was always the state of the Serbs. I know that well and you know that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberkic. Yesterday during the examination-in-chief or, rather, the day before yesterday, you said that on the day of the outbreak of the conflict you had set out for the hospital and you came across some roadblocks. Where were these roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first roadblock was in Donja Polje - that's a part of town that's called that - and the other roadblock was near the KP Dom at the bridge called Donja Drinski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, is it correct that you said that you came across a Muslim who wore a TO uniform, a Territorial Defence uniform?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain this to us? What kind of a uniform is this, a TO uniform?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think those are the police uniforms from before the war, blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it was primarily Muslims there. Did you see a single Serb at that roadblock?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other roadblock by the bridge on the Drina, who held that roadblock?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice any men there. There was only one truck there and it was hard to pass by. However, I didn't notice any armed men or anybody in general. I didn't notice any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the road leading to the hospital, this road that goes by the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you said, or at least that's the way I understood you, that when the conflicts broke out up to the 20th, when -- until the Serb -- until the Serb military came to the hospital, there were no Serb doctors or staff at the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not express myself that way. I said that most of the things that were done at the hospital, and I mentioned specifically which wards I was referring to, were carried out by Muslim doctors and nurses. However, there were Serb doctors and nurses too. And I never made a statement to that effect, that there were no Serb doctors or nurses in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about patients, only Muslims or also Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: While the witness is waiting to answer that question, may I remind you, Mr. Bakrac, you have to pause too. You're coming in well and truly before the end of the translation, I'm afraid. I know it's difficult, but do try.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Patients in the hospital at that time were both Serbs and Muslims, and there were probably others as well. Probably there were some Croats too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You mentioned a person called Adnan Isanovic, that he was wounded in the chest and that Dr. Torlak said to you that due to the bleeding in his chest, he had to be operated on urgently. You said that after that, you heard that this person was shot behind the hospital. Do you know whether the surgery was actually performed or not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was performed, but I'm not absolutely sure about that. I saw him only once. I talked to him. That's what I stated. But I think the surgery was not performed, although I repeat I'm not absolutely sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you discussed this with Dr. Torlak and Isanovic, how many days later did the Serb army take the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly how many days had gone by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, since you said just now that it is primarily the Muslim medical staff that was working at the hospital, why was this person not operated on?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly because I don't know whether surgery was performed on him at all or not; that is to say, I don't know why surgery was not performed on him, if it was not, nor do I know who operated on him if there was an operation. I said I talked to him only once and that surgery was needed, but whether it was actually done, why not and why yes, I really don't know. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, you're a doctor. If his chest -- if there was bleeding in his chest, how long could he go on without an operation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the blood vessel that was injured, which part of the chest too, and how fast blood is flowing into the chest cavity. However, at any rate, if the patient has breathing problems, surgery has to be performed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Berberkic. You said that in the village of Josanica, joint guards were organised. Did you take part in this guard duty?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I never stood guard in my life except in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps my question is going to be a longish one and it may require a lengthy answer, so perhaps this would be a good time to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would be a good idea. Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. We'll resume again at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, can you follow me? Are your headphones on?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break we talked about Josanica. You told me you were not on guard duty, in response to my question. In the area of Josanica, were there Territorial Defence units consisting of Muslims? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a group of people, about 40 of them, but I don't know how they called themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that you said in your statement there were 60 of them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's possible. Yes, maybe 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you said that on the day you were wounded you were on your way searching for your relative, and that is how you got wounded. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for my brother and for my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to remind you, Mr. Berberkic, that in the statement you gave to the OTP, you stated that you were wounded when you were on your way trying to locate people from the Territorial Defence. Which of the two is true? And you also said that you had got lost in the woods.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to find my brother and my brother-in-law who were in the woods and I got lost, that much is true; but I don't know whether they were members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know whether your own brother and brother-in-law were members of the Territorial Defence? Isn't that a bit odd?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that moment, the Territorial Defence did not exist as an organised group of people in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said there were about 60 people, so you allowed the possibility that there were 60 men organised as Territorial Defence in that area.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a group of people who were trying to defend themselves. How they called themselves, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were wounded, was there your brother or your brother-in-law with you, or were you alone?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't alone. Aziz Merkez was with me -- I'm sorry, it's not Aziz, it's Halim Merkez. There was my brother-in-law, Nedzad.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last name of Nedzad.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Dzahid Spahicanin, but my brother wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. The interpreter didn't hear the last name of the second person -- I'm sorry, the third person you referred to, Nedzad. What is the last name that you used?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last name is Delic, Nedzad Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those persons who were with you when you were wounded, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were wounded, who did you give your pistol to?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave it to my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To Nedzad Delic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they arrested the same day as you were?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, since you are from Josanica, do you know what happened to the Serbian population on the 19th of September [as interpreted], 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake in the transcript. 19th of December, not September.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was then imprisoned in the KP Dom, but I heard there was an operation, an attack on Josanica, and a large number of Serbian civilians were killed. That is what I was told by the guards in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, you mentioned that you watched the incident in Filipovici in the barracks through the binoculars. You said that four to five persons were killed on that occasion, executed by a firing squad. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I stated precisely is that four or five persons were singled out and that I heard shots. Whether they were killed at that moment, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you watch that from?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the village of Kradazici, which is on the right bank of the Drina River, and it is on the same level as the military facility in Filipovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see where those five or four persons were taken to.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken behind the barracks, behind the military installation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, did you state that you heard later that some of them had run away, some of the people who were taken behind the barracks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I later heard that one of those who were to be shot had survived, had run away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said it was more than one.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one person survived, but, of course, people tell stories. Somebody says it's one, another person will say it's two, but I believe one person survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We will now move on to the role of the accused, Krnojelac, in the KP Dom. I will read out to you a part of your statement given to the OTP. On page 5 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 6 - and today in your examination-in-chief you also mentioned two prisoners with the same first and last names, that is, Dzevad Lojo - you said you had heard from them that the warden of the KP Dom was Milorad Krnojelac, and that he was the one in charge of you. "In my room there were two detainees called Dzevad Lojo. Both of them had talked to Krnojelac. I believe that was in the summer of 1992, about three or four months after my arrival at the KP Dom. These two men with the last name of Lojo later told me that Krnojelac had told them that he did not control the situation and that the military command decided Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. everything. He said that the staff of the prison was in the service of the military command and that he could not help, but he promised to improve the living conditions of the camp." Can you please tell us which things -- which of the things are true? What is true, what you said in your examination-in-chief or what you stated to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does "OTP" mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I give this statement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave this statement to the Prosecutor's office on the 14th and 15th of December, 1998, and the date of reading is the 7th of September, 1999?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some illogical things here. With me in the room there was Dzevad Lojo, the director of the mine in Miljevina, who was closer -- who knew Krnojelac better from before the war. The other man was not together with me in the room at the time, and I'm speaking about Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, today once again you mentioned the two men with the same first and last names from whom, as you said, you received information about the administration of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at that moment Dzevad Lojo, the director of Maglic, was not with me in the room. I later met him in another room. I believe that was in Room 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you are not pausing before answering or questioning, and you are making it very difficult for the interpreters, so please remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The essence of my question, sir, is not whether he was in the room with you. I just read out to you what you stated as having learned from both these men. I'm asking you what is true, what you said today in your examination-in-chief or the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said quite clearly that I got this information from one and from the other, but at that moment they were not in my room. All I have here is the information I gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on this transcript of mine, but at this moment I cannot remember exactly what I said earlier today. And you are asking me to say in detail what I said today as opposed to what I said two years ago, and to define any difference there may be between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I'll try to make my question easier. What I read in your statement, is it true that you said that to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Also, you said earlier today that you used to see Milorad Krnojelac in daytime, in the afternoon, very often in the evenings, and twice when there were alerts. I will read out to you a part of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe I misunderstood or the translation was wrong, but the witness never said that he saw Krnojelac in the evenings. He said he only heard from the judges -- sorry, from the guards, from the guards that he was supposed to be there. He never said during his direct examination that he saw him in the evening, just on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That may be so. It's certainly my recollection that he did not refer to having seen him himself, but if you've got something in the transcript, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow us, my colleague Mr. Vasic will try to find it. That is, at least, what we heard. Maybe it's a matter of interpretation. But I should like to read a very short sentence to the witness, and he will confirm whether it is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I saw him in the prison only during the day. Sometimes in the evening when there were test alerts he was also present." So here in the statements you say explicitly that you saw him only during the day. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said, that I saw him during the day at various times of the day, in the morning, around lunch, and in the afternoon, but I did not see him on any night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you say in any of your statements so far that it was the guards who drew your attention to the fact that Milorad Krnojelac was around since you were talking about the subject anyway?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that no one asked me directly where and from whom I got the information that he visited the camp during the night. No one ever asked me that question in any of the sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree, sir, but they did ask you when Milorad Krnojelac was present in the KP Dom. Why didn't you mention that he came during the night as well, if you had such information?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I believe primarily what I see so that I couldn't answer this question otherwise at that moment. I think that is very simple, a very common sense answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who those two guards were who told you that Milorad Krnojelac was also present during the night.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can name at least two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the guards with whom I could talk, [redacted] and [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have found, I think, the passage that you may have been thinking of at page 27 of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you saw Mr. Krnojelac on other occasions in the KP Dom. Did you ever see him in the evening?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did come to the compound in the evenings. I don't remember it. I don't remember if I personally saw him within the compound, but I believe he did come. He was asked what the basis of his belief was, and he went on to describe that the guards were always more careful when he was in the premises. I think that's the only one. I don't think he ever said what you suggested he said, but if you can find another one, you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I owe you an apology, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not to me. No, you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that in your statements given to the Office of the Prosecutor you mentioned conversations with Mitar Rasevic as well?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us today about the subject of these conversations. However, I will tell you what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor on page 8 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 1: "Rasevic sometimes talked about my brother. Sometimes Rasevic would say that he received orders from the command. I heard that the military commander was someone named Kovac. The father of the two detained brothers Cemo tried to organise their exchange. He communicated with Kovac through ham radio. The brothers received a message to the effect that their father was unable to organise the exchange due to problems with Commander Kovac." You said today, and you never said this before, that Rasevic had told you that it was in the jurisdiction of the warden. Which is true?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I stated today is more accurate than what is written here. I remember very well my conversation with Rasevic on both occasions, and what I stated today is the truth. I think, however, that he tried or, rather, it was through him that this conversation with the Cemo brothers took place. I don't know how it came about that I apparently stated that some Kovac was a military commander. I don't remember ever stating anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will try to refresh your memory, sir. You didn't mention him just once. And you also said today that you spoke to Gojko, the nurse. I will read out to you the end of the second paragraph on the same page: "Gojko, the nurse, said that anything that was done in the prison required permission of Commander Kovac." Is it helpful to you? Did it refresh your memory or do you continue to maintain that you never said this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a date to it when Gojko said this? Is any date mentioned in the statement? I remember very well stating to the Office of the Prosecutor that on one occasion I asked Gojko to help us improve the situation and help us with the treatment of detainees, especially elderly ones, and he said that he was not in a position to and that the administration of the prison did not allow it. However, I don't remember this part. I think something is wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is wrong? You didn't say this and the Office of the Prosecutor wrote it of their own accord or what?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is a complete misunderstanding. There was a ham radio amateur by the name of Kovac who tried to organise this exchange, but I don't recall any Commander Kovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you stated that Gojko, the nurse, said that anything that was done in the prison could be done only with the permission of the commander, Kovac. And who was this ham radio operator then? Where is the logic in it? If I try to tell you, just in order to refresh your memory, that the commander of the Foca Tactical Group was named Kovac, would you still stand by your claim that it was a ham radio operator?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then there are two men with the last name of Kovac and one of them is a ham radio operator for sure, and he tried to organise the exchange of the Cemo brothers. Then both of the brothers were in the same room with me, and they told me about it. As for Colonel Kovac or whatever, it's probably some kind of confusion with names or a misunderstanding of some kind, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's have a look at the transcript. "I never said Colonel Kovac." How did you get that one, that it was a Colonel Kovac? Actually, he is a colonel, but I was wondering how come you came up with that if you're not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again that I know about a ham radio operator Kovac who was working on this exchange, and I think that he was some kind of a mountaineer before or something like that and that he came to the camp to work on this exchange. As for a Colonel Kovac, I don't know whether any such person exists. I don't know. Maybe this person introduced himself as "Colonel." I really don't have any idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to point out that, actually, counsel mentioned Colonel Kovac at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He certainly referred to him as "Commander." I don't remember a "Colonel," but I haven't gone all the way through. Have you got a reference to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. We have just found the point, but it's actually the witness mentioning it. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. By your leave, Your Honour, just one more question in relation to this because we aren't getting anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should just once again read out very briefly a clear sentence which shows that there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. The interpreters cannot follow him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From time to time Rasevic would say he was getting orders from the command. I heard that the military commander was a certain Kovac. I don't see what is not clear here.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat once again that I talked to Enver Cemo and to the other Cemo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about Enver Cemo. I'm asking you about what you said concerning this conversation with Rasevic. Can you answer me about that, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In his previous statement, the witness did not mention that Mr. Rasevic spoke about Kovac. The witness actually said, "Sometimes Rasevic mentioned that he got orders from the command. I heard that a certain Kovac was the military commander. The father of the two detained brother Cemo tried to arrange an exchange for his sons."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Everybody who reads always speeds up, it's a very natural reaction, but it creates havoc for the interpreters, and the typists, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "The father of the two detained brothers Cemo tried to arrange an exchange for his sons. He communicated with Kovac with the help of a radio amateur." That is what I would point out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's something which probably is something more in re-examination. But nevertheless, where are we getting with this? It seems to me, if I may say so, Mr. Bakrac, you're doing the very thing that I was trying to stop Mr. Vasic from doing yesterday, and that is going through every minor little variation in the statements, between that and the evidence. It really doesn't help us very much unless it relates to a matter of some importance, and you have referred to some matters of importance, but most of these seem to be so much on the periphery of the issues of this case that it is not going to help us that the witness has refined his evidence or he's changed it in a minor way. Do you think we can stick to what are the important issues, and if there's some sort of a variation between his statements and his evidence, you draw them to our attention as they will be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am really worried by the fact that this question, the question related to the chain of command, is unimportant. I just wanted to react as my learned friend was reading that there are full stops in between. She read it all together, because there is a full stop after, "I heard that there was a certain Kovac who was a military commander," then it says full stop, and then -- however, if there is any kind of confusion concerning the Cemo brothers, I'm going to put another question which I believe is not confusing. Gojko the nurse said that the consent of commander Kovac was needed for everything that took place in the prison, so there is nothing unclear about this. There's a full stop, and then comes a new paragraph that deals with different questions, so let the witness answer that. Did the OTP not register his statement properly, or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know. But you have now, I think, brought us to the issue where it may be important, but we have been travelling a long way to get there. You proceed in relation to the chain of command by all means, but until you read that part out, I'm afraid it seemed to have nothing to do with what we're concerned with. Now if there is some commander or Colonel Kovac who was in charge of the goings on in this KP Dom, you go ahead and establish it, but please, let's get on to that and leave the other immaterial variations to one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence will present evidence in this direction during its own case, and that is why we believe that this particular point is so important in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I've just read this other sentence of yours to you from your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statement. You said that Gojko, the nurse, told you that the permission of commander Kovac was needed for everything that was to be done within the prison.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this? When did I give this statement? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave this statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 14th and 15th of December, 1998, and the date of reading is the 7th of September, 1999.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the accuracy of this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never said that to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in this position, I cannot confirm the accuracy of this statement or, rather, I cannot be sure that I said this in such a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, I'm going to refresh your memory a bit more now, so I'll put it to you this way. On page 12 of this very same statement, in the second paragraph, the first sentence reads as follows: "In June in 1993 when the Red Cross visited the KP Dom, 12 of us were hidden. Enver Cemo saw a list with 12 names. The list had been signed by Marko Kovac." Is it a ham radio operator that signed this list?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who this is, but this information is correct, and this statement of mine is absolutely accurate. Who Marko Kovac is, though, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, and you repeated it here also during your examination-in-chief, that Gojko Jokanovic personally told you that he could not help you because the administration would not allow that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and he repeated that on several occasions, not only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement on page 7 you said, "A male nurse, a Serb by the name of Gojko, was in charge of us. Dr. Torlak and the other detained physicians asked him for help, but he answered that he was not allowed to help." You did not say here that you talked to him, and you did not say that it was the administration that had forbidden him to help.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement is correct. I don't know why I didn't say it then, but it's not only Dr. Torlak, Dr. Karovic, Dr. Berberkic who talked to Gojko; everybody did. I absolutely assert that I talked to him, and I talked to him several times about it. I said that. And I say once again that he said quite clearly that it was the administration that had forbidden him to help. He used that word quite clearly, the "administration." He did not mention any names, nor did I insist then, because that really would have been a bit too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we are discussing the nurse Jokanovic anyway, you said that detainees went to the clinic and stole medicine. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That was one of the ways in which we managed to keep some medicines for emergency cases. The only way to do this was to hide them away from him so that he would not know that we had these medicines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you to the clinic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards who were on duty, those who were on duty that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they take you to the clinic if it was forbidden, if Gojko was forbidden to help you? And why was he there every day, anyway, if he was not allowed to help you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what I could say to that. I have no specific opinion with regard to this question. I think, I think -- I said it earlier on too, that he tried to do everything that was within his power and that he could have got into trouble on account of that. He said to me several times --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you why you were taken to the clinic. The guards could have told the administration that he was helping you, that you were being taken to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People complained of various illnesses. People needed help badly. I'm talking about the quality of medical assistance. I think that the quality of medical assistance was not adequate or at the level that these detainees deserved. Again, I say that Gojko did everything that was within his power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just tell me something else. Do you know the name of Dr. Dobrilovic? You mentioned Dr. Vladicic, Dr. Kostovic, if I remember well, Dragovic. Do you know the name of Dr. Dobrilovic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Dobrilovic? I think his first name is Milovan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he came to the prison once or twice, but I cannot remember. I think he was there twice or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you thought that these doctors came once a week. Do you allow for the possibility of this having taken place twice a week?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was not regular. I don't think that it was twice a week, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, you said here that you were taken to an isolation cell because of a pair of socks that you had made for yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you never mention that before, neither to the OTP nor to the security centre in Sarajevo? You said that you spent the night in an isolation cell, that is to say, only one night, when there was that incident concerning a slice of bread. You never said this to anyone.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again, they probably did not ask me, and I did not remember at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, how many times were you in solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once, because of the pair of socks that I had made for myself. This other time, I was not in solitary confinement, and I don't know where that statement came from. Again it's probably a confusion with terms or time or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Savo Todovic took you to eat when there was this incident with bread.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Todovic took me to the canteen and said that I could eat. I ate, but I could not eat very much. Then I was taken to an isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an answer to this, Dr. Berberkic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in isolation only once. I think it was because of this pair of socks, or whether it was this other time, I can't define that for you clearly, but I think it was on account of the socks. I'm convinced it was because of this pair of socks. How come it came up here, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, Mr. Berberkic, we were talking about food. Is it correct that at the time when you were detained in the KP Dom there was a general shortage of food?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, there were no food shortages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, I am going to read part of your statement to you now. On page 6 of the B/C/S version, the last paragraph, just one sentence: "The fact that we got little food had nothing to do with the fact that there was a general shortage of food."

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what I think? I think that the translation into English was wrong or that there was some kind of a language misunderstanding. I said several times that there was enough food, that there was food in storage, that there was flour in the basement of the bakery where we spent one day but that this food had never reached the detainees. I stand by that. I assert that with full responsibility. You put to me a very equivocal question a few minutes ago and it can be interpreted in two different ways, both in terms of yes and in terms of no. You asked me, more or less, whether it was correct. I mean, I don't have to interpret this for you now. I said that there was not a shortage of food. Isn't that right? But you did not say whether this was in prison or in town. You did not ask me that, so please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I'll ask you. In town?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat your entire question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the town of Foca, while you were detained, was there a general shortage of food?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about food, you said that in the warehouse of the KP Dom, you saw macaroni and rice and tinned food; is that correct? Does that mean that you never got macaroni or rice or tinned food?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got macaroni and rice most of the time. As for tinned food, we did not get tins, especially not anything like ham or salami or something like that. And the quality of food is obvious due to the fact that so many detainees, all the detainees, lost lots of weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberkic. You mentioned a person called Mr. Esad Hadzic, and you said that he was carried out wrapped in a blanket, that he had died due to an ulcer perforation. Did he die in the hospital or the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to Dr. Torlak, when he was transferred to my room, about Esad Hadzic. I think that he had had an ulcer perforation sometime in the afternoon - that's what Torlak told me - and that he was carried to hospital only the next morning. So it is probable that he died in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked about the incident in the yard with the soldiers, you said that you think that these were soldiers from Bileca and that you understood that because of the way they spoke. What is the distance between Foca and Bileca in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the distance is in terms of kilometres, but I know that there are differences in speech. I was sure that these were not Focans. I assumed, on the basis of their accent, that they could have been from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So people from Herzegovina speak with a different accent than people from Foca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this incident last?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all of that lasted for about ten minutes, perhaps, but not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you just passing by, or were you standing there? I understood you as saying that you were passing by on your way to the canteen from your room.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that we were on our way, but we were standing in front of the canteen for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you standing there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we would always form lines in front of the canteen, that is one reason; and the other reason is that the guards ordered the detainees to bow their heads and keep them down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is how you stood for ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say it seemed like an eternity to me, but I don't believe it was more than ten minutes - I'm repeating this again - because I thought they would use their weapons and shoot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you stood there for at least ten minutes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't have a watch to time it, nor did I have anything else, nor did I have a sense of time at all, but it certainly is about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You spoke about Nedzad Delic, Hasan Dzano, and Emir Mandzo. These three men, do they come from the same place?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from the same place, but places in the same neighbourhood, very close to one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly as saying they were neighbours?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are from different villages, but I repeat, those villages are very close to one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they arrested on the same day?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzad Delic -- no, no, no, they were not arrested on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take part in the Territorial Defence, and did they possess weapons?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Emir Mandzo was brought in from the hospital ward where he worked; Hasan Dzano allegedly turned himself in; and Nedzad Delic, my brother-in-law, was arrested on the same day that I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberkic. I would appreciate the usher's help in showing you the floor plan of the KP Dom, and I would like you to tell me about the solitary cells in the administration building which you mentioned. Can you please show us exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 6/A, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6/A, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are Rooms 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For purposes of the transcript, the witness is showing solitary cells as being located in the administrative building, to the right from the entrance, in the building marked as "administrative building," and those are the second and the third rooms on the right-hand side marked 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, relative to the metal door through which you have to go in order to enter the administrative building from the compound, can you show me what you call the right-hand side of the building and what you call the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when entering from the compound, from inside?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What do you understand to be the right-hand side and what is the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left-hand side is this office, Room 1 and Room 2. That is the part of the building where the administration was, and to me, this is the left-hand side. The right-hand side is opposite. This is the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness is indicating the left-hand side of the building as the part of the administrative building where the words "administrative building" are written, and containing rooms marked as "office," Room 1 and Room 2; whereas he identifies the right-hand side of the building as the part which is left from the main entrance to the KP Dom where the words "the guards' building" are written, zgrada straze.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. Bakrac, that when I read that in the transcript tomorrow I will be completely lost. I understood the witness to be adhering to the attitude he expressed the other day that he's looking at it from what he saw from inside the KP Dom itself, so that what shows on the left-hand side of the plan was what he was describing as the right side of the building, and what appears on the right side of the plan he saw as being on the left-hand side because he was inside the KP Dom. Now, I don't think he has said anything differently, has he?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for this clarification. It is more helpful to the Chamber because you're reading the transcript, but I will ask another question which is actually the reason why I have asked this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, when you were talking about incidents, you said in your statement on page 9, "At the time when these incidents took place, the guards were not in their usual workplaces, on their usual posts. That's why I believe all of them were involved. I am sure that all of these incidents took place on the ground floor in the right wing of the administrative building where the solitary cells are."

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which incidents do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the beatings of detainees which you mentioned in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have been only in the left part of the building, not in the right. They interrogated people in the left-hand side of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you stated to the Office of the Prosecutor in your statement, which I have already mentioned, is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one detail missing. From where are you looking? From inside the prison or outside?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you observe these beatings from, from the inside?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Room 16. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means you were observing them from the inside, and you just gave us your explanation as to what the right and the left sides are.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left-hand side of the building, in my understanding, includes Rooms 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that the beatings took place in the right-hand side of the building. In your examination-in-chief, you said they happened in the left-hand side of the building. I want to know which one is true.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on how you phrase the question relative to the entrance to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberkic. Speaking about the beatings, you said you saw people being taken out. Were they taken out in groups or individually?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please ask a direct question? You mean taken out from their rooms or taken out from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From their rooms, into the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the June, July --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: June, July, the period you discussed.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken out in groups of two to four men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These groups of two to four men, would they be taken through the metal door together or some of them waited in front of the metal door? Correction: Would they be taken through the door at once or would they wait?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were cases when the detainees waited in front of the metal door for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps remember who waited outside the metal door?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say by name, not with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time of day did these -- would people start being taken out?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, after lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time would that be?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was after 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these beatings lasted until 10.00 or 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So two to four people were beaten from 3.00 to 11.00 p.m., and during all that time, you would hear cries for help and screams?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 3.00, not only one but several groups would be taken out, three to four groups, and that would amount to about 15 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the 28th of June, in the evening, you heard shots. Where did these shots come from? Where did they seem to be coming from?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they came from the rooms which I identified as Rooms 1 and 2 and from outside the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you heard not less than five shots. How many of them came from inside those rooms and how many came from outside the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not clearly define or distinguish how many came from outside and how many from inside the rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said during your examination-in-chief that the next day you also heard shots but those were individual shots, single shots. What did you mean by that? Does it mean that those five shots you heard on the 28th were a burst of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the shots were single shots. It was not automatic fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you mean then by saying that on the next day you also heard shots but those were single shots?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many shots did you hear the next day and where did you hear them from?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which day do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the day after the 28th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I stated that I heard shots the next day. I don't know where I could have stated that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that during your examination-in-chief when my learned friend asked you about these incidents. Did you hear shots on the next day or didn't you? Try to remember now, please.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I can't confirm this statement with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberkic. Tell me, please, on the 28th of June when you heard those shots, which detainees had been taken through the metal door?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names of the detainees. I cannot remember, but I know that they belong in a group of 30 men who were taken out. The names of the people who were taken out on the 28th of June is something that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember it was the 28th of June, you remember that you heard not less than five shots, you remember that some of them were inside, some of them in front of the building, you remember that 30 or so men were taken out, but you cannot remember any one of them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I cannot claim with any certainty. I can give you the names, some names if you want me to, but I don't want to say things of which I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberkic. Could you tell us if you ever mentioned to the Office of the Prosecutor or the security services centre in Sarajevo the coat of Mr. Uzunovic and that you received it through some channels later on?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, but even if I didn't, my statement about that coat is absolutely correct, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you never mentioned it before, at least, not in those statements that are available to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there are a lot of things which I never said and which I will never say, so I see nothing odd in some things coming up just like that because one question evokes new memories, and I see nothing strange about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berberkic, what did you do with that coat when you received it somehow?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wore it for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it covered with blood?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was completely bloody with bloodstains in the upper part on both the right and the left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a doctor's coat or a raincoat?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the raincoat which he wore to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to tell that it was his coat?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the same ward and I saw him in that same raincoat in the prison as well while he was in building number 1 and when he was being taken out. There is absolutely no doubt, no chance that it could be another man's coat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was [redacted], Witness FWS-76, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have a request to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- on behalf of this witness. We just received messages from, from our other staff, and they are in contact with the Witness/Victim Unit, and they informed us that this witness has to return to his home tomorrow. He has to fly out. He came already twice now, and he already spent an entire week here, and according to the information, he's used his entire leave that he got from his employer, and now he is in big trouble if we do not finish. So I wonder if we could proceed for a little while further on today, or maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I wish you'd raised this a bit earlier. We've got no opportunity to consult with those who matter in these matters, and those are the people who have very strict time limits on the periods during which they can work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd actually not expected this to happen because we had consulted with Defence counsels and we expected this to end, actually, within 45 minutes, and I -- actually, till now I was always wondering when does it stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How long do you think you will be, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise to my learned friend. I said that we don't have any time evaluations in our system, and the answers came more slowly than I expected them to. I'll try to abbreviate the rest of my questions, and I believe we can finish within five or ten minutes, if that is acceptable to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's see how we go with the interpreters and the typists. Ten minutes? I wish we had had less of the irrelevant cross-examination and we would have got through in time. Is there any problem with the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ten minutes would be all right, say the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Or the typists?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, but the Prosecution would have, let's say, five minutes for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think if they're not worried about 10 minutes, they won't be worried about 15 minutes, but let's just see how we go. That doesn't mean to speed up any questions, that will cause their own problems, but let's try to shorten the questions themselves. You proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
